idiom_name: unexported package functions + one orchestrating function (methods only when the receiver is needed)
implementation_notes: Go has no classes and no `private`: the unit of hiding is the package, so the steps of a composed method become unexported functions (`func computeTotal(...)`) or unexported methods on the type, while the outline stays one exported function or handler whose body is a list of calls - Effective Go's requirement that a function be named for what it does is exactly this discipline. What replaces the classic private-member structure is package scope plus multi-return values: a step returns `(T, error)` instead of writing through an out-parameter, so its contract is visible at the call site, and unexported helpers remain testable from a same-package test file. Prefer a plain function when the step needs no receiver, because that keeps the type's method set (and any interface it satisfies) small; use a method only when the step depends on receiver state.
pitfalls: Every step returning `error` makes the outline a chain of three-line checks; that is idiomatic Go, but it also invites discarding a failure with `_` or wrapping the same error twice - handle at the outline and wrap once with `%w` so the identity survives.

Package-private helpers are reachable from every file in the package, so tests drift into calling steps directly and freeze the implementation; keep tests at the outline's seam unless a step has a contract of its own.

Long parameter lists are the Go smell that a boundary is wrong - when three helpers thread the same five values, introduce a named struct (a Parameter Object) or attach the step to a type instead of adding parameters.
